parsed_answer.content:
In production Java systems, particularly when dealing with complex Exception Handling & I/O / NIO pipelines, mastering pure functions and side-effect management is non-negotiable for writing predictable, concurrent, and thread-safe code. A pure function is a deterministic routine where the return value is identical for identical arguments, and it strictly executes without mutating any external state or triggering observable side-effects. By contrast, real-world I/O operations—such as reading from a non-blocking FileChannel, writing to a SocketChannel, or throwing checked exceptions when a buffer overflows—are inherently side-effecting because they interact with the operating system kernel, modify global heap states, or mutate network buffers.

Managing side-effects effectively requires decoupling the core business logic, which should ideally reside in pure, referentially transparent functions, from the imperative outer shell that handles side-effects like file I/O, database writes, and error logging. In asynchronous NIO architectures, side-effects also manifest as state mutations inside selectors and byte buffers. If multiple threads concurrently modify a shared ByteBuffer without explicit synchronization or thread-confinement strategies, data corruption ensues. Therefore, handling exceptions gracefully in this environment means encapsulating volatile network and disk interactions using monadic containers or structured functional wrappers, ensuring that errors are treated as first-class values rather than abrupt control-flow disruptions.

rows: Always returns the same output for the same input
Output depends on external state (disk, network, clock)
Zero mutation of external variables or heap state
Mutates global state, files, memory buffers, or handles
Errors represented as returned values (e.g., Either, Try)
Throws checked or unchecked exceptions abruptly

items: Referential Transparency allows compilers and developers to substitute a function call with its resulting value without altering program behavior, significantly simplifying automated testing and parallel execution.
NIO Selector interactions and ByteBuffer mutations inherently violate purity because position, limit, and mark pointers are mutable state variables managed internally by the buffer instance.
Side-effect containment patterns push I/O operations to the absolute edges of the application architecture, isolating the impure code while keeping domain logic clean and unit-testable.

parsed_answer.content: A common production trap in NIO programming involves passing shared ByteBuffers into multiple asynchronous pipelines. Because buffers maintain mutable pointers (position, limit), concurrent reads and writes without thread-confinement or duplication via ByteBuffer.allocateDirect() will lead to race conditions and corrupted data streams. Always treat buffer allocation and pointer manipulation as side-effects that require strict isolation.
